title: The Lantern of Nagasaki's harbor
premise: In 1898, Mirabel Marchetti tends the lighthouse above Nagasaki's harbor, hiding the truth that her late husband was Italian-born but that she herself sheltered a Japanese naval officer's family during the last peacetime summer. When census taker Elias Thorn arrives asking questions tied to rising anti-foreign sentiment and a missing ledger of harbor contacts, Mirabel must choose between burning her dead husband's promise to the Hara family or exposing herself as a collaborator. As storms batter the coast and suspicion closes in, she smuggles the Haras' youngest son out of the city aboard a coal barge, sacrificing her position and nearly her life. The book ends with the century turning: Mirabel, stripped of her post but not her purpose, lights a private lantern on the headland each night until the Haras return to tend it beside her.
about_author: F. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former merchant marine who spent years in East Asian port towns collecting oral histories from lighthouse families. Their fiction blends archival research with the salt-worn cadences of sailors' letters home.

chapters.title: The Weight of Glass
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. She polishes the great lens and catalogs her routines, revealing through small details the death of her husband Tomas and her careful invisibility. Emotional beat: grief disciplined into habit, with an undercurrent of dread at the approaching census season.

chapters.title: A Man with a Ledger
chapters.summary: Census taker Elias Thorn arrives at the lighthouse, polite but persistent, noting discrepancies in the household record. Mirabel deflects. His POV briefly shows he is hunting something specific—a list of names. Beat: first contact; the reader feels the trap closing.

chapters.title: What Tomas Promised
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Mirabel's POV. The peacetime summer of 1895: Tomas and Captain Hara sealing a friendship over sake, the promise that the Marchettis would always shelter the Hara family if politics turned. Beat: warmth shadowed by dramatic irony.

chapters.title: The Storm Season Opens
chapters.summary: The first great storm of the year strikes; Mirabel keeps the light burning alone through the night. Thorn shelters at the station, probing her past under cover of courtesy. Beat: forced intimacy with danger; she realizes he knows more than he says.

chapters.title: Kenji at the Door
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Kenji Hara, nineteen, appears soaked and desperate—his father detained, his mother hidden in the city. Mirabel takes him in against every instinct for survival. Beat: the promise becomes flesh; fear and loyalty collide.

chapters.title: Two Plates, One Table
chapters.summary: Quiet domestic tension as Mirabel teaches Kenji lamp work while concealing him from supply boats. Kenji's POV reveals his guilt over his father's arrest. Beat: fragile found-family warmth that the reader knows cannot last.

chapters.title: Thorn Returns
chapters.summary: Thorn arrives unannounced with questions about 'foreign nationals harbored in coastal stations.' Kenji hides beneath the lantern room floor. Mirabel lies for the first time cleanly. Beat: the price of survival begins accruing interest.

chapters.title: The Harbor Whispers
chapters.summary: Mirabel visits the fish market for intelligence and hears that the Haras' name is on a watch list—and that informers are paid in rice. An old friend warns her. Beat: paranoia spreads; trust becomes currency.

chapters.title: Letters Never Sent
chapters.summary: Mirabel reads Tomas's old letters and finds coded references to the Haras, realizing Thorn may already possess similar papers seized from the harbor office. Beat: memory turns from comfort to liability; the past is evidence.

chapters.title: The Coal Barge Bargain
chapters.summary: Mirabel negotiates with gruff barge captain Okafor to carry Kenji to Shanghai after the next storm clears the patrols. He demands payment she doesn't have. Beat: desperation meets pragmatism; a plan forms on borrowed time.

chapters.title: What Thorn Wants
chapters.summary: Thorn's POV. We learn his own wound: a brother lost to a scandal he blames on foreign sympathizers, driving his zeal. He suspects Mirabel but hesitates. Beat: antagonist humanized; the moral stakes complicate.

chapters.title: Midnight Repair
chapters.summary: A storm damages the lens mechanism; Mirabel and Kenji repair it together through the night, hands bleeding, laughing once despite everything. Beat: the emotional high before the fall—the closest thing to joy the book allows.

chapters.title: The Informer
chapters.summary: A supply boat boy glimpses Kenji and reports it. Mirabel learns the net is closing within days. She must move the escape up or abandon it. Beat: ticking clock engaged; panic sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: Burning the Letters
chapters.summary: Mirabel burns Tomas's letters to destroy the evidence, weeping as twenty years of memory go up the chimney. Beat: the theme made literal—to survive, she must destroy what she loves most.

chapters.title: Interrogation by Lamplight
chapters.summary: Thorn confronts Mirabel with the harbor ledger page bearing Tomas's signature. She neither confirms nor denies, offering him instead a story about mercy that visibly shakes him. Beat: climax of words; loyalty vs. truth fought in a single room.

chapters.title: The Night of the Third Storm
chapters.summary: The worst storm in decades hits as Kenji slips down to the barge. Mirabel must keep the light burning for the ships—including the patrol boat—while her whole future rows away in darkness. Beat: split-screen suspense; duty and love pulling opposite directions.

chapters.title: Wreck on the Shoals
chapters.summary: A patrol boat founders near the shoals; Mirabel's light guides rescuers, saving the very men hunting Kenji. Thorn arrives drenched and changed. Beat: ironic grace—her fidelity to the lamp saves her enemies and shames the hunt.

chapters.title: The Choice at Dawn
chapters.summary: Thorn finds Kenji's abandoned coat and understands everything. In silence, he pockets the evidence instead of filing it, asking only why. Mirabel answers: 'Because someone kept a promise to me once.' Beat: quiet climax; mercy answered with mercy.

chapters.title: Relieved of Duty
chapters.summary: Officialdom strips Mirabel of the keeper's post regardless—her independence itself was the offense. She packs Tomas's sea chest and walks down from the headland. Beat: loss without bitterness; survival's price paid in full.

chapters.title: The Lantern on the Headland
chapters.summary: Mirabel rents a fisherman's hut and sets a small lantern in its window facing the sea, lighting it nightly. Neighbors begin to say the old keeper never stopped working. Beat: ritual as resistance; memory transformed into devotion.

chapters.title: Return with the Tide
chapters.summary: Spring, 1900. A boat carries Kenji and his freed father back across the harbor. They find Mirabel's window lit and take up the watch beside her. Beat: the promise honored across years; reunion earned, not given.

chapters.title: What the Light Remembers
chapters.summary: Final chapter, Mirabel's POV, years later. An aging Mirabel tells a young visitor which stories are true and which are kind inventions, insisting both matter. The lens of the old lighthouse gleams in the distance. Beat: resolution on memory itself—truth survives best when tended like a flame.
